# ISLA: an invariant slice-attention surrogate {#sec-mt2}

ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention; the code class is `ISLA`) is a soft-slice
transformer for steady boundary-value problems whose backbone never sees a
coordinate. Every learned operation acts on rotation- and
translation-invariant scalars built from the boundary geometry and the
problem's global condition vectors, and vector outputs are assembled at the
very end from an equivariant basis. In every experiment of this book the
problem is external aerodynamics and the one global vector is the freestream
direction; the architecture itself knows only that a global unit vector was
supplied. The result is a surrogate whose
rotation and translation covariance is exact by algebraic construction
rather than learned (verified to roundoff in float64; the residual of the
bf16 training path is a measured quantity, @sec-mt2-contracts), whose
parameter count matches GeoTransolver's (8.9M vs 9.0M), whose training step
on the path the recipe runs costs 1.05x GeoTransolver's at 10,000 tokens in
half the memory (@sec-mt2-cost), and whose in-distribution accuracy is at or
below that of the unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver on every surface
rung measured (@sec-scoreboard). What it adds is a set of exact contracts
and a reference frame that reads nothing from the sample, so that its
prediction is consistent under a change of surface sampling where every
configuration that centres on the sampled points is not
(@sec-scoreboard-consistency); no single part of the design is load-bearing
for its own accuracy (@sec-mechanism). This chapter describes what ISLA
computes, states its contracts as the tests that verify them, and prices
each design choice with the measurements from the results chapters.

ISLA pays for symmetry once at the network's edges (invariant inputs,
equivariant output basis) and spends the interior on the routing
mechanism that has the strongest empirical record on industrial
aerodynamics, the soft-slice attention of the Transolver family
(@sec-baselines). The opposite trade, enforcing physical structure inside
every layer with typed scalar/vector streams and analytic
boundary-integral kernels, fails on separated 3D flow
(@sec-interior-negatives).

## What goes in and what comes out {#sec-mt2-architecture}

**ISLA maps a sampled boundary plus the problem's global condition vector
to fields at query points, and every field it produces transforms with the
input under rigid motions.** The inputs, per case, are:

- a set of $N$ sampled boundary points $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ (10,000 per
  case in the protocol of @sec-protocol);
- the unit outward normal $n_i$ at each point;
- a measure weight $w_i > 0$ per point: the surface area the point
  stands for, so that $\sum_i w_i f(x_i)$ approximates $\int f \, dA$;
- one global condition vector $d \in \mathbb{R}^3$, called the *drive*: a
  direction that belongs to the problem rather than to any boundary cell.
  In this book's external-aerodynamics datasets it is the freestream
  direction; for a buoyant flow it would be the gravity direction. The
  current implementation takes exactly one such vector and requires it;
  problems with no global direction (steady conduction with pinned
  temperatures) or with several are outside what the shipped code accepts
  today, and generalizing the drive to a list of zero or more global vectors
  is the engineering step that would admit them (@sec-limits);
- optionally, per-cell boundary data (`boundary_scalars`), the channel for
  whatever a boundary condition prescribes at each cell, and per-query
  scalars (`query_scalars`), used in this book for the signed distance to
  the wall.

The outputs are one or more scalar fields (surface pressure in every
result in this book) and one or more vector fields (wall shear stress)
at query points. In the reference configuration the queries are the
surface sample itself and each point receives its own prediction. With
the passive decoder enabled (`query_independent=True`), queries may be
any positions, on or off the surface, and the prediction at one query
does not depend on which other queries are evaluated.

Three properties hold by construction, independent of training:

1. Rotating and translating the inputs rotates the vector outputs by the
   same rotation and leaves the scalars unchanged. Translation invariance
   needs no centering: no centroid appears anywhere in the reference
   configuration's forward pass.
2. Rescaling the geometry uniformly (points scaled by $k$, areas by
   $k^2$) changes nothing, because the only length unit is the square root
   of the total surface measure. The constant-gauge variant
   (@sec-mt2-variants) is instead invariant to multiplying every measure
   weight by the same constant and *not* to a geometric rescale; the two
   properties trade places with the choice of scale (@sec-mt2-contracts).
3. In the passive-decoder mode, the prediction at a query is a function
   of the surface sample and that query alone.

@sec-mt2-contracts states each property as the test that verifies it.

## The forward pass {#sec-mt2-forward}

**Every stage below is either a fixed geometric map or a learned map
acting on invariants; the two never mix until the output basis.** The
stages describe the reference configuration (`frame_mode="relative"`,
`scale_mode="total_measure"`, the class defaults); the two gauge variants
that differ from it are collected in @sec-mt2-variants. The symbols are
tied to the identifiers in `physicsnemo/experimental/nn/isla/model.py`.
Every constructor argument and every `forward` input is keyword-only, so a
call reads as the recipe's `forward_kwargs` mapping does and models can be
swapped without positional bookkeeping.

| symbol | code | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x_i, n_i, w_i, d$ | `points`, `normals`, `measure_weights`, `drive` | inputs: positions, unit normals, cell areas, the global condition vector (the freestream direction in this book's datasets) |
| $L$ | `gauge` | length scale: the square root of the total quadrature measure of the sample |
| $r_i, \hat n_i, \hat d$ | `r`, `n_hat`, `d_hat` | scaled position (used only in differences), and unit directions of normal and drive |
| $\ell_i$ | `log_w` | log measure weight, the bias that makes routing quadrature-weighted |
| $s_i$ | `invariants` | the invariant seed per point, $\hat n_i\cdot\hat d$ |
| $h_i$ | `h` | hidden state per point, width 192 |
| $\lambda_{is}$ | `logits` | routing logit of point $i$ to slice $s$; $S = 256$ slices |
| $a_{is}$ | `a` | routing weight, normalized over points for each slice |
| $z_s, m_s$ | `z_pos`, `m_s` | equivariant anchors: weighted mean position and mean normal of slice $s$ |
| $g_{is}$ | `geo` | the six relational invariants of point $i$ against anchor $s$ |
| $Z_s$ | `z` | slice state: the measure-weighted mean of $h$ over the slice |
| $\pi_{is}$ | `point_mix` | read-back weight, normalized over slices for each point |
| $b_i, \gamma_i$ | `back`, `geo_pool` | what a point reads back: slice states and pooled relational invariants |
| $\hat u_i$ | `r_hat` (head) | unit direction from the token's soft slice anchor to the token, the radial basis vector of the vector head |
| $e_\theta, e_\phi$ | `spherical_basis` | tangential basis vectors completing $\{\hat d, \hat n, \hat u\}$ |

### Frame and length scale

The reference configuration has no frame origin. Positions are divided by
one length,

$$
L = \Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^{1/2}, \qquad r_i = x_i / L,
$$

the square root of the total quadrature measure of the sample, which is
the total surface area, an integral of the geometry. Under
Horvitz–Thompson weights this estimate is consistent under any sampling
law, so nothing about where the mesher placed its cells enters the scale.
$r_i$ itself is never used alone: every later stage consumes differences
$r_i - z_s$ against slice anchors, so a common shift of all points cancels
exactly and translation invariance holds without centering. A uniform
rescale of the geometry (points by $k$, areas by $k^2$) scales $L$ by $k$
and leaves every $r_i - z_s$ unchanged, which is the scale contract of
@sec-mt2-contracts. Unit directions are $\hat n_i = n_i/\lvert n_i\rvert$
and $\hat d = d/\lvert d\rvert$.

### Invariant seed

Each point enters the backbone as one scalar,

$$
s_i = \hat n_i\!\cdot\!\hat d, \qquad h_i^{(0)} = \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{embed}}(s_i),
$$

the orientation of its normal relative to the drive: the only rotation
invariant of $\{\hat n_i, \hat d\}$ that does not refer to a position. A
point's location is supplied entirely by the slice layers, which measure
it against anchors. The measure weight enters as a log-space bias,
$\ell_i = \log w_i$ (zero if weights are absent or
`use_measure_weights=False`).

### Measure-weighted soft-slice routing

Each of the 12 pre-LayerNorm slice layers (`_SliceBlock`) routes every
point to every slice with a softmax over *points*:

$$
\lambda_{is} = W_a\, \mathrm{LN}(h_i), \qquad
a_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda_{js} + \ell_j)}.
$$

The bias $\ell_i$ turns each slice's aggregate into a quadrature rule:
$\sum_i a_{is} f_i$ is a weighted mean whose weights are proportional to
$w_i$ times a learned, content-dependent factor. Adding a constant to
every $\ell_i$ cancels in the ratio; in the reference configuration the
same constant also rescales $L$, which is why the reference is invariant to
a joint geometric rescale rather than to a weight rescale alone
(@sec-mt2-contracts).

### Equivariant anchors

From the routing weights each slice forms two vectors,

$$
z_s = \sum_i a_{is}\, r_i, \qquad
m_s = \frac{\sum_i a_{is}\, \hat n_i}{\big\lvert \sum_i a_{is}\, \hat n_i \big\rvert},
$$

a weighted mean position and a mean normal direction. Both are linear
in equivariant inputs with invariant weights, so they rotate with the
body. They give the layer 256 data-adaptive reference points; a point's
position is then described by its relation to this constellation
rather than by coordinates in any frame.

### Relational invariants, routing refinement and read-back

For every point–anchor pair, with $\rho_{is} = r_i - z_s$ and
$\hat\rho_{is} = \rho_{is}/\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert$, the layer forms six
invariants:

$$
g_{is} = \big[\,
\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\ \log\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat d,\ \hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat n_i,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\! m_s,\ \hat n_i\!\cdot\! m_s
\,\big].
$$

All six are relational: the distance to the anchor, the direction cosines
of the separation against the drive, the point's normal and the anchor's
normal, and the alignment of the two normals. Because $\rho_{is}$ is a
difference of positions, a common shift of the sample cancels here
exactly. A linear map of $g_{is}$ to one scalar refines the routing,
$\lambda'_{is} = \lambda_{is} + w_g\!\cdot g_{is} + b_g$, and the routing
weights are recomputed with the same measure-weighted softmax. The slice
state is the routed mean of the hidden states, passed through a
per-slice MLP:

$$
Z_s = \sum_i a'_{is}\, h_i, \qquad Z_s \leftarrow Z_s + \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{slice}}(\mathrm{LN}(Z_s)).
$$

Reading back uses a softmax over *slices* (no measure bias, since a
point is choosing where to read, not how much it weighs):

$$
\pi_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda'_{is})}{\sum_t \exp(\lambda'_{it})}, \qquad
b_i = \sum_s \pi_{is}\, Z_s, \qquad
\gamma_i = W_f \Big(\sum_s \pi_{is}\, g_{is}\Big) + b_f,
$$

$$
h_i \leftarrow h_i + W_b\,[\,h_i;\ b_i;\ \gamma_i\,], \qquad
h_i \leftarrow h_i + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(h_i)).
$$

The order of operations in $\gamma_i$, pool the invariants over
slices and then project to width 96, is what sets ISLA's memory footprint
(@sec-mt2-cost). The point ends the layer knowing
which slices it belongs to, what those slices contain, and where it sits
relative to their anchors.

### Passive decoder

With `query_independent=True`, the encoder above runs unchanged on the
surface sample and its final state is summarized once: a final
measure-weighted routing gives slice states $Z_s$ and anchors
$z_s, m_s$ from the last hidden states. Each query $q$ with position
$x_q$ and normal $n_q$ is placed in the same length scale, $r_q = x_q/L$,
seeded with the same invariant seed, and passed through four read
blocks (`_ReadBlock`). A read block forms the same relational
invariants $g_{qs}$ against the final anchors, routes over slices,

$$
\pi_{qs} = \mathrm{softmax}_s\big(W_a\,\mathrm{LN}(h_q) + w_g\!\cdot g_{qs}\big), \qquad
h_q \leftarrow h_q + W_b\,[\,h_q;\ \textstyle\sum_s \pi_{qs} Z_s;\ W_f \sum_s \pi_{qs}\, g_{qs} + b_f\,],
$$

and then reads the encoder states near the query with a
measure-weighted Gaussian kernel of width $\varrho$ (`local_readout_rho`,
0.02 length-scale units),

$$
u_q = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, e^{-\lvert r_q - r_i\rvert^2/\varrho^2}\, h_i}
{\sum_i w_i\, e^{-\lvert r_q - r_i\rvert^2/\varrho^2}}, \qquad
h_q \leftarrow h_q + W_l\,[\,h_q;\ u_q\,],
$$

followed by the residual MLP. Nothing in a read block writes into
$h_i$ or $Z_s$, so the map from encoder state to $h_q$ is a function of
$x_q$, $n_q$ and the source alone. For queries off the surface
(`interior_queries=True`, @sec-interior) a normal is synthesized
equivariantly as the soft assignment of $r_q$ to the anchors
$z_s$ applied to the anchor normals $m_s$; explicitly supplied
`query_normals` override it.

### Scalar and vector heads

A single linear head on the normalized final state produces the scalar
outputs and, for each vector output, seven coefficients:

$$
[\,p_i;\ c_{i}\,] = W_h\, \mathrm{LN}(h_i), \qquad
v_i = \sum_{k=1}^{7} c_{ik}\, B_{ik}, \qquad
B_i = \big\{\hat d,\ \hat n_i,\ \hat u_i,\
e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat n_i),\ e_\phi(\hat u_i, \hat n_i),\
e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat d),\ e_\phi(\hat u_i, \hat d)\big\}.
$$

The radial basis vector $\hat u_i$ is the unit direction from the token's
own soft anchor to the token: a dedicated routing head assigns the token
to slices, the slices' measure-weighted mean positions are formed as in
the layers, and $u_i = r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is} z_s$ with $\beta_{is}$ the
token's softmax over slices. It is a difference of positions, so the head
stays translation covariant without a centre. Here $e_\theta(\hat u,
\hat a)$ is the component of $-\hat a$ orthogonal to $\hat u$ and $e_\phi =
\hat u \times e_\theta$, both left unnormalized so that they vanish
smoothly where $\hat u \parallel \hat a$ and no direction field on the
sphere has to be combed. The three input directions already span
$\mathbb{R}^3$ generically; the four complements make the expansion well
conditioned when they are nearly coplanar. All coefficients are invariants
and all basis vectors are covariant, so $v_i$ rotates with the input.
Finally the whole output is multiplied by $\lvert d\rvert$; the recipe
supplies a unit direction, so this factor is identically one and carries
no physical content.

### The gauge variants {#sec-mt2-variants}

**Two documented variants replace the frame-free reference frame with a
frame estimated from the sample; both are selected by
`frame_mode="centered"` and both carry the sample's point distribution into
the forward pass.** They share one centred construction, which subtracts a
centre $c$ before scaling, $r_i = (x_i - c)/L$, and differs from the
reference in three places:

- the seed is five scalars instead of one, the complete rotation
  invariants of $\{r_i, \hat n_i, \hat d\}$ up to parity,
  $[\lvert r_i\rvert, \log\lvert r_i\rvert, \hat r_i\cdot\hat d,
  \hat r_i\cdot\hat n_i, \hat n_i\cdot\hat d]$ with
  $\hat r_i = r_i/\lvert r_i\rvert$; the four that refer to the centre are
  what the reference removes;
- the relational invariants are eight instead of six: two that describe
  the anchor's position relative to the centre, $\lvert z_s\rvert$ and
  $\hat z_s\cdot\hat d$ with $\hat z_s = z_s/\lvert z_s\rvert$, are
  broadcast to every point and carry the centre into the routing;
- the head's radial basis vector is $\hat r_i$, the direction from the
  centre, instead of the direction from the token's soft anchor.

**The constant-gauge variant** (`scale_mode="reference_length"`,
`center_mode="plain"`) centres on the plain mean of the sampled points and
scales by a constant,

$$
c = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i, \qquad L = L_{\mathrm{ref}} = 8.0,
$$

with `reference_length` in the recipe's nondimensional units (the recipe
divides coordinates by a per-case reference length before the model sees
them, 5 m on DrivAerML, so 8.0 is 40 m physical there). The plain mean is a
mesher statistic: under a 10:1 sampling-density bias it moves by a large
fraction of the body length and every downstream invariant leaves its
trained range (@sec-robustness-density). This variant is behind the
constant-gauge columns of the results chapters.

**The similarity-gauge variant** (`similarity_gauge=True`) replaces the
plain mean and the constant by the measure-weighted centroid and the
measure-weighted RMS radius,

$$
\tilde w_i = \frac{w_i}{\sum_j w_j}, \qquad
c = \sum_i \tilde w_i\, x_i, \qquad
L = \Big(\sum_i \tilde w_i\, \lvert x_i - c\rvert^2\Big)^{1/2},
$$

integrals rather than point averages, so they do not move when the
sampling density is redistributed; it is exactly equivariant to a
geometric rescale and remains a frame estimated from the sample.
@sec-mt2-design prices both variants against the reference.

## Contracts, as tests {#sec-mt2-contracts}

**Each contract is a property of the code, verified in double precision
on random weights and a random anisotropic point cloud, not a property
of a trained checkpoint.** The tests live in
`test/experimental/nn/test_isla.py` (46 tests, several parametrized; the
tests of the gauge variants pass `frame_mode="centered"` explicitly and
`test_default_is_relative_total_measure` pins the default). The fixture is
a 3-layer, 32-slice, width-64 model in fp64 on 500 points with random
normals, drive and weights; tolerances are absolute.

| test | assertion | tolerance |
|---|---|---|
| `test_rotation_equivariance` | for a random proper rotation $Q$: scalars unchanged, vectors $v \mapsto vQ^\top$ | $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_translation_invariance` | shifting all points by a constant leaves every output unchanged | $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_relative_frame_contracts` | reference configuration: shifting all points by a constant leaves every output unchanged with no centering; rotation covariance; points $\times 2.5$ with areas $\times 2.5^2$ leave every output unchanged while areas alone do not (the total measure *is* the length unit); one seed and six relational invariants; the excluded combinations raise | $10^{-12}$ / $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_default_is_relative_total_measure` | `ISLA()` with no frame arguments is the relative frame with the total-measure scale | exact |
| `test_measure_weight_scale_invariance` | gauge variants: multiplying all $w_i$ by 137 leaves every output unchanged | $10^{-9}$ |
| `test_drive_degree_one` ($k \in \{0.5, 2, 4\}$) | scaling $d$ by $k$ scales every output by $k$ | $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_collated_input_shapes` | drive as $(B,1,3)$ or $(3,)$ gives the same output as $(B,3)$ | $10^{-12}$ |
| `test_query_set_independence` | passive decoder: same source, 50 queries alone vs the same 50 plus 100 others; the shared predictions agree | $10^{-12}$, rtol 0 |
| `test_qi_rotation_equivariance`, `test_qi_drive_degree_one` | rotation and drive contracts hold in the passive-decoder configuration | $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_anchor_conditioned_decode_query_independence` | with a fixed interacting anchor subset (`n_anchors`), query independence and rotation covariance both hold | $10^{-12}$ / $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_interior_queries_contracts` | off-surface queries with no normals: rotation covariance, translation invariance, query independence, finite outputs | $10^{-10}$ / $10^{-12}$ |
| `test_similarity_gauge_geometric_scale_equivariance` | similarity-gauge variant: points $\times k$, areas $\times k^2$ and a shift leave the output unchanged ($k = 2.7$); the constant-gauge variant changes its output by more than $10^{-3}$ under the same rescale | $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_local_rotation_equivariance`, `test_local_drive_degree_one`, `test_boundary_scalar_channel_contracts`, `test_scale_conditioning_rotation_equivariance`, `test_latent_volume_tokens_contracts` | the optional feature channels (local patch integrals, boundary scalars, scale conditioning, latent volume tokens) preserve the rotation and translation contracts | $10^{-10}$ |
| `test_geo_pool_then_project_is_exact` | pooling the relational invariants over slices then projecting equals projecting then pooling, for both block types | $10^{-12}$, rtol 0 |
| `test_geo_checkpoint_is_exact` | rebuilding the per-slice geometry inside the backward pass gives the same outputs and gradients as storing it | exact (outputs) / $10^{-11}$ (gradients) |
| `test_all_parameters_receive_gradients` (5 configurations) | every parameter receives a gradient (a requirement of distributed data parallel) | exact |
| `test_head_variants_run_under_bf16_autocast` (3 heads) | the head variants run and backpropagate under bf16 autocast with finite outputs | finite |
| `test_a35b_ablation_flags_run_and_differ`, `test_raw_coord_channel_breaks_equivariance_by_design` | the flags of the single-factor ablation at 35 training cases (@sec-mechanism) each run, give finite outputs and change the prediction; `use_relational_geo=False` stays exactly equivariant; `seed_mode="raw"` and `raw_coord_channel` break rotation covariance by more than $10^{-3}$, which is their purpose | as stated |

The rotation test uses a proper rotation ($\det Q = +1$). Under a
*reflection* the picture is asymmetric, and the tests say so
explicitly. Every invariant in the backbone is a norm or a dot product,
so scalar outputs are exactly invariant under reflections as well.
Two of the seven basis vectors, $e_\phi(\hat u,\hat n)$ and
$e_\phi(\hat u,\hat d)$, are cross products and therefore flip sign
under a mirror while their coefficients do not; the default vector head
is covariant under rotations and translations only, and
`test_parity_fix_reflection_equivariance` asserts that it is *not*
mirror-covariant. Three alternative heads are exactly O(3)-covariant
and verified as such (`parity_fix`, which gates the $e_\phi$
coefficients with the pseudoscalar $\hat u\cdot(\hat n\times\hat d)$;
`vector_basis="true5"` and `"true7"`, which drop or replace the
pseudovectors; `odd_head`, which builds parity-odd coefficients from
triple products against the slice anchors). None is the reference head;
their measured cost is collected in @sec-limits.

What is not a contract:

- **Measure-weight scale alone.** In the reference configuration the
  total measure is the length unit, so multiplying every $w_i$ by a
  constant without rescaling the positions changes the output, and the
  relative-frame test asserts that it does. What is invariant is the
  joint rescale of a geometry (positions by $k$, areas by $k^2$). The
  gauge variants have the opposite pair: invariant to a uniform weight
  rescale; invariant to a geometric rescale only with the similarity gauge.
- **Reflection covariance of vectors**, as above.
- **Drive degree.** The output scales linearly with $\lvert d\rvert$ and a
  test confirms it, but the recipe feeds a unit direction, so the factor
  is one in every training and evaluation run. It is a normalization
  detail, not a physical law: in the aerodynamic instance a pressure
  coefficient is degree zero in the freestream speed and a dimensional
  pressure is degree two, and a gravity vector's magnitude would enter a
  buoyant problem through a dimensionless number, not this factor. ISLA has
  no drive-magnitude contract.
- **Query independence in the reference configuration.** Without the
  passive decoder, every surface point is an interacting token, so the
  prediction at a point depends on the rest of the sample. On DrivAerML
  at matched token counts the dependence is measured at 6.8% relative
  change of the prediction at a shared 5,000-cell prefix when the
  companion points change (GeoTransolver 2%). The exact contract is
  bought by the passive decoder at the price stated in @sec-mt2-design.
- **Refinement of the source measure, in the query-token configuration.**
  In the interior configuration whose queries interact as tokens
  (@sec-interior), each query's routing weight is a learned factor times
  the *geometric mean* of the source weights. Splitting every source cell
  into two halves of half the area leaves every integral against the
  discrete source measure unchanged but halves every query weight, so the
  balance between surface and queries shifts: in a float64 probe on small
  random models the outputs move by 3.7% (query tokens) and 9.1% (query
  tokens with the signed distance) where the plain surface model moves by
  8e-16. The same convention makes the query count, the query distribution
  and chunking part of the effective measure, and the measure-weight and
  geometric-scale contracts (uniform rescalings of all weights, or of the
  whole geometry) do not detect this. The interacting decode's prediction
  at a point therefore depends on the joint query set: count augmentation
  during training reduces the dependence on the request size by about 40%
  at a 3.7% cost and does not remove it, so the interior model is deployed
  at its training query count (@sec-nb-qcount-verdict,
  @sec-nb-relint-verdict). A convention in which the total query mass is a
  learned fraction of the total source measure, divided by the query
  count, removes the dependence on refinement and count by construction.
- **Composition of optional channels.** Each optional channel preserves the
  rotation and translation contracts on its own (table above), but not
  every pair composes: the similarity gauge together with the surface
  local-feature channel is not scale-equivariant (the patch log-mass is not
  normalized by the length scale, so a 2.7x rescale moves the output by up
  to 0.79 in the probe where the gauge alone is at roundoff); the passive
  decoder together with boundary scalars, scale conditioning or raw seed
  features fails with a shape error when the source and query counts
  differ; and the passive decoder with the parity-odd vector head collides
  on the normals when they differ. None of these combinations is behind
  any number in this book, and the plain reference surface configuration
  is unaffected.
- **Completeness of the invariant representation.** The slice anchors are
  first moments (measure-weighted mean position and mean normal) of the
  points routed to a slice, and the seeds and relational invariants are
  built from them. Two arrangements whose transverse first moments about
  the drive vanish can therefore be indistinguishable to every layer even
  when they are not congruent: five equal spherical components at azimuths
  {0, 120, 240, 27, 207}° and {0, 120, 240, 43, 223}° about an axial drive
  have different pairwise-distance profiles and no rotation carrying one to
  the other, and ISLA's outputs on the common component agree to 4e-15
  (reference and similarity-gauge configurations, two seeds); the optional
  local-distance channel separates them (0.039–0.063), as does a
  second-moment channel (`second_moment_features`, 2.41 against 1.99)
  (`results/isla_first_moment_collision_2026-09-08.json`). Rotational
  symmetry about the drive is thus sufficient but not necessary for the
  collision. Either channel removes it at a known cost
  (@sec-nb-mom2-verdict); it is a documented representation limitation and
  is not established as the cause of any measured deficit on cars or wings.
- **Finite-precision residual on the deployed path.** The contract tests
  run in float64; the recipe trains and evaluates under bf16 autocast. A
  CPU autocast probe of the scalar rotation residual gives 1.2–1.3% in
  bf16 against 6e-7 in float32 and 1e-15 in float64, so "exact" describes
  the algebraic construction; the residual on the GPU trained path is a
  quantity to be measured rather than asserted, and it is not yet measured
  (@sec-program-status).

## Cost {#sec-mt2-cost}

**At the recipe dimensions (hidden 192, 12 layers, 256 slices) ISLA has
8.9M parameters, against GeoTransolver's 9.0M. On the path the recipe runs,
both models compiled, one GB300, bf16 autocast, batch 1, 10,000 tokens and
the AdamW step included, ISLA's training step is 1.05x GeoTransolver's (47
against 45 ms) at half the peak memory (1.30 against 2.70 GiB) with the
geometry recompute on, and 0.86x (39 ms at 1.94 GiB) with it off.** The
step is memory-bound at every stage but the MLP: the relational invariants
alone move 61% of the step's memory traffic, which is why the eager path is
slower than the compiled one and why the ratio grows with tokens. At 40,000
tokens the default compiled step is 2.2x GeoTransolver's (119 against 53
ms); an exact fused kernel for the geometry region, opt-in as
`geo_kernel="fused"`, brings it to parity (52 ms) at 4.5 against 10.0 GiB,
and the compiler's autotuned mode alone brings it to 41 ms. Every option in
@tbl-mt2-cost computes the same function (output relative L2 against the
eager reference at most 5.5e-7 in bf16, 1e-15 in fp64).

| ISLA execution path (10,000 tokens) | step [ms] | ISLA ÷ GeoTransolver step | peak memory, ISLA (GeoTransolver) [GiB] |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| compiled, geometry recompute on (the recipe's default) | 47 | 1.05x | 1.30 (2.70) |
| compiled, geometry recompute off | 39 | 0.86x | 1.94 (2.70) |
| compiled with the fused geometry kernel (`geo_kernel="fused"`, opt-in) | 45 | 1.00x | 1.27 (2.70) |
| eager, geometry recompute on | 87 | 1.28x | 1.52 (4.07) |
| eager with the point softmax in its middle-dimension layout (`fast_point_softmax=False`) | 245 | 3.61x | 1.52 (4.07) |

: Training-step cost of ISLA's execution paths against GeoTransolver on the same path (compiled or eager), one GB300, bf16 autocast, batch of one case, 10,000 tokens, AdamW step, median of measured steps; memory is the peak allocated during the step. The last row is the layout the trained checkpoints ran and is the source of every larger ISLA step-time ratio measured before the compiled path (@sec-nb-kernel-study). Data: results/kernel_study_2026-09-13/pareto_gb300_full_bf16.json. {#tbl-mt2-cost}

The passive decoder adds four read blocks (1.1M parameters, 9.9M total;
4.9 GB reserved by the training logger at 10,000 interior queries) and the
query-token interior configuration adds only a type embedding and a routing
weight (8.9M total; 6.0 GB reserved and 0.28 s per step at 10,000 interior
queries, because the per-slice geometry spans every token); neither is part
of the configuration behind the surface accuracy numbers
(results/v0_interior_resources_2026-09-07.json).

Where the memory goes. Hooking every tensor autograd stores for the
backward pass and grouping by shape, about three quarters of the stored
activations at 10,000 tokens are per-slice geometry: the (points × slices
× 3) separation vectors and their unit versions, the (points × slices ×
6) invariants, and the (points × slices) distances and routing softmaxes;
the token path (hidden states, MLP activations) is the remaining quarter.
Every geometric tensor is a cheap elementwise function of five small
inputs: the point positions, normals and drive direction (points × 3 each)
and the anchor positions and normals (slices × 3). The recipe therefore
rebuilds them inside the backward pass instead of storing them
(`geo_checkpoint`, one recompute region per layer covering the routing bias
and the pooled invariants). The forward output and every gradient are
bitwise identical to the stored-activation path under bf16 autocast, and
peak step memory falls 2.3x for a 1.16x step time on the eager path
(results/isla_memory_recompute_2026-09-07.json; @sec-nb-geo-recompute); the
compiled path shows the same trade in @tbl-mt2-cost. What remains is the
token path and the (points × slices) routing softmaxes themselves, which
are the one per-slice quantity the backward pass genuinely needs.

Why the ordering of two operations decides the footprint. Each slice layer
holds the pairwise invariants $g_{is}$, a tensor of shape $(B, N, S, 6)$,
and uses them twice: once mapped to one routing logit per pair, once
pooled over slices with $\pi_{is}$ and mapped to a width-96 feature per
point. ISLA pools before projecting. The alternative ordering, projecting
each pair to width 96 and then pooling, would require autograd to save the
projected tensor $(B, N, S, 96)$ for the backward pass: at $N = 10{,}000$
and $S = 256$ that is $2.5\times10^8$ elements, about 0.5 GB in bf16, per
layer, or 5.9 GB across 12 layers. The projection is affine and $\pi_{is}$
sums to one over slices, so

$$
\sum_s \pi_{is}\,(W_f\, g_{is} + b_f) \;=\; W_f \sum_s \pi_{is}\, g_{is} \;+\; b_f ,
$$

and pooling first produces the identical tensor while saving only
$(B, N, 6)$. The same identity applies in the read blocks. The contract
test checks it at $10^{-12}$ on both block types, and at the model level
the two orderings with identical weights differ by $4\times10^{-15}$ in
fp64, so checkpoints are interchangeable between them. The per-pair
projection would also cost about 2 GFLOP per layer each way, so pooling
first saves step time as well as memory. With it, the $(B, N, S, 6)$
invariants and the $(B, N, S, 3)$ separation vectors are the dominant
activations, and ISLA's memory is close to linear in tokens per case.

## Design choices and their measured cost {#sec-mt2-design}

**No single ingredient of ISLA carries its accuracy; the largest single
effect measured is 16%. The reference frame buys consistency under a change
of surface sampling at a price of 0 to 14.5% against the constant-gauge
variant, depending on the rung, and exact query independence costs
3.0–3.7x.** Each choice below carries one headline number and a
cross-reference to the chapter that defines the measurement and reports
the full readout. The ablation numbers are ratios of a variant's pressure
error to the constant-gauge variant's (0.138) in the single-factor ablation
at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases under the frozen protocol of
@sec-protocol, two seeds; greater than one means the variant is worse
(@sec-mechanism).

**Relational routing** is the largest single contribution. Removing the
anchor invariants from routing and read-back (`use_relational_geo=False`,
Transolver-style feature-only slicing) costs 1.16x at 35 cases
(@sec-mechanism).

**Exactness of equivariance** is a contract, not the source of the
accuracy. Appending raw coordinates to the seeds (`raw_coord_channel`)
costs 1.04x and replacing the invariant seeds by raw vectors
(`seed_mode="raw"`) gives 0.99x, so adding coordinates does not help;
every variant keeps an invariant path through the relational invariants,
so these ablations do not show that invariants are dispensable. What the
contract removes is the need for a canonical frame or a global-direction
estimate at inference, and it earns 6% and 19% against augmented
GeoTransolver and Transolver when geometries arrive in arbitrary poses
(@sec-pose).

**The frame** reads nothing from the sample, and that is what makes the
prediction consistent under a change of sampling. Under a 10:1
sampling-density bias on DrivAerML the reference frame degrades 1.2x where
every configuration that centres its coordinates on the sampled points,
whichever architecture it belongs to, degrades 10 to 16x
(@sec-scoreboard-consistency). The constant-gauge variant's collapse is its
plain-mean centroid and nothing else: the same trained checkpoint evaluated
with a measure-weighted centre goes from 12.1x to 1.12x
(@sec-nb-centroid-derivation, @sec-nb-center-probe-verdict;
`results/center_probe_2026-09-10.json`). Under refinement the
measure-weighted ISLA's convention-swap penalty converges from 2.9x at
2,500 cells through 1.45x to 1.05x at 40,000, while the released baselines
stay at 3 to 7x (@sec-consistency-bench). The price of the reference frame
against the constant-gauge variant is 0% on DrivAerML, 1% and 5% at 4 and
21 training geometries (never-seen validation geometries), 11% at 35 and
210 cases, where the validation geometries recur in training, and 14.5% at
the fixed angle (three seeds); on both splits tested with an exact
full-geometry frame the price is the plain mean's mesher pattern (its
centroid sits 0.131 body lengths off the geometric one on the wings, 0.034
on the cars), not positional information (@sec-nb-frame-full-verdict,
@sec-nb-frame-full-fixed-angle-verdict, @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-verdict).
The similarity-gauge variant costs 1.08x at 35 cases against the
constant-gauge variant and also holds at 1.2x under the bias
(@sec-robustness-density); it is a frame estimated from the sample, and the
reference is preferred at equal accuracy.

**Measure weights** are a correctness requirement, not a tunable. With the
cell-area log-weights in the routing softmax, a slice aggregates an integral
over the surface measure, so the output does not depend on how the surface
was sampled; without them it aggregates a mean over whichever points the
mesher placed, and a uniformly generated point cloud or a different mesher
would change the answer (@sec-principle). Turning the routing weights off
gives 0.88x at 35 cases (@sec-mechanism); that number is the
in-distribution price of the requirement, measured as an ablation and
never adopted. The price has a known mechanism and it is not in the
weights: a quadrature-weighted mean over a uniform-over-cells draw has an
effective sample size of $N/(1+\mathrm{CV}^2)$ of the cell areas, about one
fifth of the points on either dataset, so each slice state is a noisier
estimate of the same integral and moves about twice as much when the
surface is resampled (@sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe, @sec-limits-mechanism).
That variance part shrinks with cell count and is nearly gone at 40,000
cells on DrivAerML; the part that does not shrink, on the wings, is
mesh-pattern content the ablation learned from the mesher, and under an
area-proportional draw it collapses to errors worse than predicting zero
(@sec-nb-bench-verdict, @sec-consistency-bench). The cure consistent with
the requirement is more cells at evaluation, not dropping the weights;
retraining under an area-proportional draw, which makes the weights
constant, does not buy the advantage back (@sec-limits-mechanism).

**Query independence** costs 3.0–3.7x on DrivAerML surface pressure
(@sec-query-independence). The passive decoder reaches 0.203–0.211
against 0.0577 for the interacting constant-gauge variant at learning rate
1e-3, the 3.5–3.7x end of the range; the anchor-conditioned variant
(`n_anchors`, a fixed interacting core with all points decoding passively)
reaches 0.209/0.221 against 0.0697/0.0671 for the 6,500-token interacting
control, the 3.0–3.3x end. The 6,500-token control is a token-count
control, not a matched-memory comparison with GeoTransolver
(@sec-mt2-cost). On the boundary→interior task the passive decode costs
3.1x on interior pressure (float32), and the interacting query-token
configuration, which gives the contract up, trails GeoTransolver's volume
configuration by 7% on interior pressure and leads it by 27% on interior
velocity (@sec-scoreboard-interior).

The flags that select these variants, and the remaining optional
channels, are listed once here so the results chapters can name them.

| flag (default) | what it changes |
|---|---|
| `frame_mode` (`"relative"`) | `"relative"` is the reference: positions enter only as point-to-anchor differences, one seed, six relational invariants, no centering. `"centered"` selects the gauge variants of @sec-mt2-variants (five seeds, eight relational invariants, a centre). Checkpoints store their constructor arguments, so a saved model loads in the configuration that trained it |
| `scale_mode` (`"total_measure"`) | `"total_measure"` divides positions by the square root of the total quadrature measure of the sample; `"reference_length"` uses the constant `reference_length` (the constant-gauge variant); `"global"` reads a supplied `frame_scale` (the full-geometry-frame diagnostic) |
| `center_mode` (`"plain"`) | under `frame_mode="centered"` only: `"plain"` centres on the plain mean of the sampled points, `"measure"` on the Horvitz–Thompson mean, `"global"` on a supplied `frame_center` (the full-geometry-frame diagnostic) |
| `similarity_gauge` (off) | the similarity-gauge variant: measure-weighted centroid and RMS-radius reference length; requires `frame_mode="centered"` |
| `use_measure_weights` (on) | log-measure bias in the routing softmax |
| `use_relational_geo` (on) | anchor-relational invariants in routing and read-back |
| `seed_mode` (`"invariant"`) | `"raw"` feeds $[r_i, \hat n_i, \hat d]$ instead of the invariant seed(s); gauge variants only |
| `raw_coord_channel` (off) | appends $r_i$ and $\hat n_i$ to the seeds |
| `query_independent`, `n_decoder_layers` (off, 4) | passive decoder with read blocks and local kernel readout |
| `n_anchors` (0) | interacting core restricted to a fixed-size anchor subset; all points decode passively |
| `interior_queries` (off) | proxy normal for off-surface queries from the anchor normals |
| `latent_volume_tokens` (off) | equivariant off-surface tokens along anchor normals; requires the passive decoder |
| `use_local_features`, `local_radii` (off) | seven measure-weighted patch-integral invariants per radius appended to the seeds |
| `second_moment_features` (off) | second-moment invariants of each slice at the query, which separate the first-moment collision of @sec-mt2-contracts |
| `n_boundary_scalars` (0) | extra per-point scalar inputs (boundary-condition traces), pass-through to the seeds |
| `scale_conditioning` (off) | appends the log raw cloud radius, deliberately breaking scale equivariance |
| `geo_checkpoint` (on in the recipe), `geo_kernel` (`"eager"`) | rebuild the per-slice geometry in the backward pass; `"fused"` selects the exact fused geometry kernel of @sec-mt2-cost |
| `parity_fix`, `vector_basis`, `odd_head` | the O(3)-covariant vector heads of @sec-mt2-contracts |

Every flag is verified by the tests of @sec-mt2-contracts to preserve
the rotation and translation contracts unless breaking them is its
purpose, in which case the test asserts the break.
